title: The Sunset Strand: Why Combing Hair After Dusk Invites Misfortune
script: As twilight paints the Indian sky, a hushed warning echoes through homes: 'Do not comb your hair after sunset.' This ancient superstition, steeped in folklore, advises against untangling your tresses once the sun dips below the horizon. Many believe it invites financial instability, loss, or even attracts wandering spirits drawn to discarded strands. Some say Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth, departs a home where such activity occurs. Others link it to practical hygiene in earlier times. A simple act, yet burdened with ages of wisdom and fear.
blog_html:
Twilight's Tangles and Lakshmi's Lament

In the vibrant tapestry of Indian traditions, where every ritual holds a story and every belief a whisper from the past, there exists a curious caution: the prohibition against combing one's hair after sunset. For generations, grandmothers have gently, yet firmly, advised against this seemingly innocuous act, linking it to various misfortunes and unseen energies.

As the sun dips below the horizon, bathing the world in hues of orange and purple, the veil between worlds is said to thin. This time of twilight, known as Gau Dhooli Bela, is considered sacred yet vulnerable. It's when good spirits retreat and mischievous or malevolent entities are believed to roam more freely. Discarded hair strands, particularly at this liminal hour, are thought to become conduits or offerings that can be exploited by negative forces. Superstition holds that these stray hairs, when combed out and left carelessly, can be used in black magic (tona totka) or attract ill-will.

A Practical Past, a Spiritual Present

Beyond the mystical, there's a practical root, too. In ancient times, with limited artificial lighting, combing hair in the dimness was difficult and led to more breakage. Sweeping up tiny hair strands in the dark was also challenging, which could contribute to an untidy home – an unwelcome sight for Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and prosperity. It is widely believed that Lakshmi blesses only clean and well-kept homes, and an act that could lead to untidiness after dusk was therefore discouraged to prevent her departure.

So, the next time twilight calls, remember this ancient wisdom. Perhaps it's a reminder to complete your chores before dark, to honour the sacred transition of day to night, or simply to safeguard your prosperity from unseen influences. Whatever the reason, the tradition of avoiding hair-combing after sunset remains a fascinating thread in India's rich tapestry of beliefs.
